Q: DefaultValueAttribute overrides values deserialized by JSON.NET after constructor A:

You've encountered some very obscure requirements of Json.NET -- some so obscure they might even be considered to be bugs. Let's take them in order:

  1. When deserializing using a parameterized constructor, Json.NET determines the metadata properties for the constructor parameter by searching for a serialized member (property or field) with the same ordinal-case-invariant name, then pulling the metadata from that property.

    Thus, if you rename a constructor parameter without also renaming the corresponding serialized field or property, certain functionality can be disabled or broken. For instance, you will lose the ability to mark constructor parameters as required, as explained in this answer to How to prevent Json.NET from using use default values for missing constructor parameters while still using default values for properties?.

    So, instead of renaming the constructor parameters, keep them the same as the field/property names, and rename the latter using attributes like so:

    [System.ComponentModel.DefaultValue("Play")]
[JsonProperty("play_button_text", DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate)]
public readonly string PlayButtonText;

  2. That being said, if you want to tell Json.NET to use a custom default value for a constructor parameter, you must apply DefaultValueAttribute to the constructor parameter directly. And you must also apply [JsonProperty(DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate)] to the constructor parameter directly. E.g.:

    public SimplifiedPlayer(
    string id, 
    [JsonProperty(DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate), DefaultValue("Play")] string playButtonText = "Play",

    I have found that neither will get picked up when applied to the corresponding property.

  3. In addition to the above, you must either mark at least one serializable member of your type as required or with DefaultValueHandling.Populate, or you must set JsonSerializerSettings.DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate for your entire deserialization session. If you don't, Json.NET will not track whether there are missing properties, and so won't determine it needs to pass in your custom default values for missing constructor arguments.

    This requirement doesn't seem to be documented, I determined it from reading through the source code of the Newtonsoft method JsonSerializerInternalReader.CreateObjectUsingCreatorWithParameters().

    The fact that this is necessary in addition to applying DefaultValueHandling.Populate to every constructor parameter feels like it might be a bug. You might want to open an issue with Newtonsoft.

Putting all this together, if I modify your SimplifiedPlayer as follows:

public class SimplifiedPlayer 
{
    const string PlayDefault = "Play";  // I added these to avoid having to type duplicated string values
    const string PauseDefault = "Pause";
    const string StopDefault = "Stop";
    
    private string ID;

    [DefaultValue(PlayDefault)]
    [JsonProperty("play_button_text", DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate)]
    public readonly string PlayButtonText;

    [DefaultValue(PauseDefault)]
    [JsonProperty("pause_button_text", DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate)]
    public string PauseButtonText { get; } // I changed this to a get-only property for testing purposes.

    [DefaultValue(StopDefault)]
    [JsonProperty("stop_button_text", DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate)]
    public readonly string StopButtonText;

    public SimplifiedPlayer(
        string id, 
        [JsonProperty(DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate), DefaultValue(PlayDefault)] string playButtonText = PlayDefault, 
        [JsonProperty(DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate), DefaultValue(PauseDefault)] string pauseButtonText = PauseDefault, 
        [JsonProperty(DefaultValueHandling = DefaultValueHandling.Populate), DefaultValue(StopDefault)] string stopButtonText = StopDefault) 
    {
        Debug.Log($"Constructing {GetType()} with arguments: {new { id, playButtonText, pauseButtonText, stopButtonText }}");
        (this.ID, this.PlayButtonText, this.PauseButtonText, this.StopButtonText) = (id, playButtonText, pauseButtonText, stopButtonText);
    }
}

It can be deserialized successfully, with PlayButtonText set to "BadLabelText" and PauseButtonText and StopButtonText set to their defaults:

string testJson = 
    """
    {
        "type": "Player",
        "start_cue": "1",
        "displayed_buttons": ["Play", "Stop"],
        "track": [1],
        "id": "P2",
        "play_once": "True",
        "play_button_text": "BadLabelText"
    }
    """;

SimplifiedPlayer test = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<SimplifiedPlayer>(testJson)!;

Console.WriteLine($"\nDeserialized {test} with contents {JsonConvert.SerializeObject(test)}");

Assert.That(test.PlayButtonText == "BadLabelText");
Assert.That(test.PauseButtonText == "Pause");
Assert.That(test.StopButtonText == "Stop");

Notes:

  • Using a record instead of your current data model is a perfectly fine workaround, it's an example of replacing a model that can't be serialized correctly with a DTO.

  • Applying Json.NET metadata overrides to constructor parameters can sometimes be tricky, see the following issues and questions for examples:

    • Json.net doesn't populate properties with default values when defined in the constructor.
    • How to prevent Json.NET from using use default values for missing constructor parameters while still using default values for properties?.
    • Json.net `JsonConstructor` constructor parameter names.
    • DefaultValueHandling.Populate doesn't set default value when deserializing #1199.
    • [DefaultValue] applied to a constructor parameter does not work when the parameter has also been renamed by setting JsonPropertyAttribute.PropertyName #3119.

Q: Which is the better way to calculate the size of one array in a for statement? A:

The generally recommended practice is that you get the count once and store it in a variable before the start of the loop (the first section of for loop). This prevents "extended" looping by mutating the array during iteration and is slightly better for performance (as of PHP 7.2, the difference is too small to be of importance for anything).

However, most people prefer to iterate over an array with foreach, which is a better choice in almost every way, except for performance. For 99.99% of the tasks, you should not be concerned with which one is faster, as their performance is so negligible that it would only make a difference if you had millions of them in your code. So for most taks you should prefer this:

foreach ($array as $element) {

}

Regarding performance: for($i = 0, $size = count($array); $i < $size; ++$i){ ... } is about 5% faster than for($i = 0; $i < count($array); ++$i){ ... } on average, but that depends on several factors. Two main factors are: whether you are on PHP 7.2+ and whether count() is fully qualified (when inside a namespace, use \count()). If that's not the case, you could even see 20% difference in performance, but all of that is useless numbers because this function is so fast that it does not matter which one you use unless you are taking part in some extreme performance challenge.

count() does not count the elements in the array each time it is called! It only returns the number of elements in the array hashtable which is O(1) operation.

Q: How can implement EM-GMM in python? A: 
# Source - https://stackoverflow.com/a/64084348
# Posted by koshy george
# Retrieved 2026-08-10, License - CC BY-SA 4.0

import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8-deep')

eps=1e-8


def pdf(data, means, vars):
    denom = np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * vars) + eps
    numer = np.exp(-0.5 * np.square(data - means) / (vars + eps))
    return numer /denom


def em_gmm(data, k, n_iter, init_strategy='k_means'):
    weights = np.ones((k, 1), dtype=np.float32) / k
    if init_strategy == 'k_means':
        from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
        km = KMeans(k, n_init='auto').fit(data[:, None]) # Added n_init for KMeans
        means = km.cluster_centers_
    else:
        means = np.random.choice(data, k)[:, np.newaxis]
    data = np.repeat(data[np.newaxis, :], k, 0)
    vars = np.expand_dims(np.mean(np.square(data - means), axis=1), -1)
    for step in range(n_iter):
        p = pdf(data, means, vars)
        b = p * weights
        denom = np.expand_dims(np.sum(b, axis=0), 0) + eps
        b = b / denom
        means_n = np.sum(b * data, axis=1)
        means_d = np.sum(b, axis=1) + eps
        means = np.expand_dims(means_n / means_d, -1)
        vars = np.sum(b * np.square(data - means), axis=1) / means_d
        vars = np.expand_dims(vars, -1)
        weights = np.expand_dims(np.mean(b, axis=1), -1)

    return means, vars


def main():
    # Generate a new synthetic dataset with three distinct normal distributions
    np.random.seed(42) # for reproducibility
    s1 = np.random.normal(loc=20, scale=2, size=50) # Cluster 1 around 20
    s2 = np.random.normal(loc=35, scale=3, size=70) # Cluster 2 around 35
    s3 = np.random.normal(loc=50, scale=2.5, size=60) # Cluster 3 around 50
    s = np.concatenate((s1, s2, s3))
    np.random.shuffle(s) # Shuffle the data to mix the clusters

    k = 3 # We know there are 3 clusters
    n_iter = 100

    means, vars = em_gmm(s, k, n_iter)
    
    colors = ['gray', 'red', 'blue', 'green'] # Changed yellow to green for better visibility if needed
    bins = np.linspace(np.min(s) - 5, np.max(s) + 5, 200) # Increased range and resolution for bins
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8)) # Increased figure size
    plt.xlabel('$x$')
    plt.ylabel('pdf')
    sns.scatterplot(x=s, y=[0.0] * len(s), color='navy', s=40, marker='o', label='Generated Data') # Changed marker
    
    # Plot the individual PDFs for each cluster
    for i, (m, v) in enumerate(zip(means, vars)):
        sns.lineplot(x=bins, y=pdf(bins, m, v).flatten(), color=colors[i], label=f'Cluster {i + 1} (Mean: {m[0]:.2f}, Var: {v[0]:.2f})')
    
    plt.title('EM-GMM Clustering with Synthetic Data')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    plt.show()

main()

Q: Running a Class.method() when that module is imported A:

You can make a decorator do what you want:

def onLoad(cls):
    cls.onLoad(cls)
    return cls

@onLoad
class Class1:
    var1 = 0

    def onLoad(cls):
        cls.var1 = 1

print(f"{Class1.var1 = }")

This code will call the method you want on the first time this is imported into your project.

You probably meant to use a @classmethod:

def onLoad(cls):
    cls.onLoad()
    return cls

@onLoad
class Class1:
    var1 = 0

    @classmethod
    def onLoad(cls):
        cls.var1 = 1

print(f"{Class1.var1 = }")
